flashcards.q: State the estimation procedure in six steps.
flashcards.a: 1) Declare what the number will DECIDE. 2) State the assumption out loud and mark it. 3) Round every input to a power of ten. 4) Compute in one pass. 5) AMPLIFY by fanout if there is any. 6) Sanity-check against a system whose scale you know; if the check fails, the assumption is wrong, not the arithmetic.

flashcards.q: The single most useful conversion in estimation.
flashcards.a: 1 million per day is about 10 per second (and 1 billion/day is about 10,000/s). 86,400 s/day rounds to 1e5, a 14% conservative error. Powers: 2^10 KB, 2^20 MB, 2^30 GB, 2^40 TB, 2^50 PB.

flashcards.q: Give the 2026 latency ladder from L1 to cross-region.
flashcards.a: L1 ~1 ns; L2 ~4 ns; L3 ~12 ns; DDR5 RAM ~50-80 ns; compress 1 KB ~1-3 us; NVMe random 4 KB read ~20-100 us; SATA SSD ~100-200 us; same-DC round trip ~0.5 ms; cross-AZ ~1-2 ms; HDD seek ~5-10 ms; US east-west ~60-70 ms; US-Europe ~75-90 ms; US-APAC ~170-230 ms; LLM first token ~300-800 ms.

flashcards.q: State the three latency ratios worth memorising over absolute values.
flashcards.a: RAM is ~1000x faster than SSD. A same-datacenter round trip is ~1000x slower than RAM. A cross-continent round trip is 100-300x a same-datacenter one. Fibre gives ~5 us/km, so ~1 ms per 100 km one-way after routing, and no engineering changes that.

NVMe Gen4 3-7 GB/s and 500k-1M random 4 KB IOPS; EBS gp3 baseline only 125 MB/s and 3,000 IOPS (about 40x slower than local NVMe); 100 GbE = 12.5 GB/s; Postgres 5-20k write TPS on one primary; Redis ~100k ops/s single-threaded (1M+ pipelined); typical JSON service ~2k rps per core; Cassandra/DynamoDB partition ~1-3k writes/s hard ceiling.

flashcards.q: Bytes per thing: the ones that come up.
flashcards.a: UUID 16 B binary but 36 B as text (2.25x waste); int64 8 B; narrow index row 40-60 B; typical entity row ~500 B; Postgres tuple overhead ~23-28 B; Redis per-key overhead 50-100 B; JSON is 2-4x protobuf; web image 100-500 KB; 1080p ~5 Mbps = 2.25 GB/hour; 1024-dim float32 embedding 4 KB (int8 1 KB, binary 128 B); 1 token ~4 chars.

Global consumer web/social 2-3x (timezone-smeared); single-region consumer 3-5x; B2B/enterprise 4-8x (ten business hours carry ~95% of load); cron/batch 10-100x; event-driven launches and ticket sales 10-1000x; notification campaigns 50-500x. Derivation: sustained peak ratio is roughly p/f where fraction f of the day carries fraction p of load, times another 2-3x for the instantaneous peak.

Peak sustained (hour) sizes the fleet and the database. Peak burst (second) sizes the queue depth, connection pool, and rate limiter. Peak concurrent (Little's Law: throughput x latency) sizes memory, file descriptors, and WebSocket capacity. Using the wrong one gives a correctly-sized fleet behind an undersized connection pool.

flashcards.q: Why size a fleet at 50-60% utilisation?
flashcards.a: M/M/1 queueing: wait = service time x rho/(1-rho). At rho=0.5 the wait equals one service time; at 0.9 it is 9x; at 0.95 it is 19x. Latency goes non-linear above ~70%, so '20% headroom' means 'our p99 is about to triple'.

flashcards.q: State the amplification rule and why it matters more than API-level QPS.
flashcards.a: Amplified writes = logical writes/s x fanout. 500 posts/s x 500 followers = 250,000 timeline inserts/s. 1M notifications/s x 1.6 channels = 1.6M sends/s. 100B messages/day x average group size 5 = 500B deliveries/day. The API-level rate is almost never what breaks; candidates who only compute it conclude the system is easy.

flashcards.q: Give the storage formula and the multipliers people forget.
flashcards.a: records x bytes x retention x replication x (1 + index overhead), then a separate line for WAL and backups. 1M records/day x 1 KB over 5 years is 1.8 TB logical, ~5.5 TB at 3x replication, ~7 TB with 30% index, and 10-14 TB provisioned once WAL and backups are counted.

flashcards.q: Nines to downtime, and the composition rule.
flashcards.a: 99% = 3.65 d/yr; 99.9% = 8.8 h/yr (43 min/month); 99.99% = 53 min/yr (4.3 min/month, so no human in the recovery path); 99.999% = 5.3 min/yr. Serial dependencies MULTIPLY: five components at 99.9% in series gives 0.999^5 = 99.5%, or 43 hours a year. Correlated failure makes the real number worse than the arithmetic.

Payload bytes are not memory. Redis adds ~50-100 B overhead per key, and a sorted set past zset-max-listpack-entries (default 128) converts from a compact listpack to a skiplist plus hash, costing ~80-120 B per member instead of 40. A naive payload calculation is typically 3x low. Verify with MEMORY USAGE and OBJECT ENCODING, not arithmetic.

flashcards.q: LLM cost arithmetic: 1M conversations/day, 6 turns, 4k input + 300 output tokens per turn at $2/$10 per M.
flashcards.a: Input 1e6 x 6 x 4e3 = 2.4e10 = 24,000 M tokens/day x $2 = $48k/day. Output 1.8e9 = 1,800 M x $10 = $18k/day. Total ~$66k/day, ~$2M/month, unviable. Levers: prompt caching at ~10% of input price (~3.6x if 80% cacheable), rerank to top-3 not top-10 (~2.7x), route 70% to a Flash-class model at ~20x cheaper (~2.5x), Batch API -50%. Composed ~24x to ~$80k/month.

flashcards.q: Vector index sizing: 100M chunks at 1024 dimensions.
flashcards.a: float32 vectors = 1e8 x 1024 x 4 B = 410 GB; HNSW M=32 adds ~300 B/node = 30 GB, so ~440 GB and it must be RAM-resident. int8 quantisation is 4x (~132 GB, one 256 GB node) for 1-2 recall points, recoverable by over-fetching top-50 and reranking. Binary is 32x (~13 GB) with a float32 NVMe rerank. Cost falls ~$5,000 to ~$700/month, so quantisation is a 7x lever. Building the index (~$800 one-time in embeddings) is 40x cheaper than serving it.

flashcards.q: What is the recovery script when you realise an assumption was wrong mid-answer?
flashcards.a: Say it immediately and precisely (name the statistical error, not just the number); do not restart; identify the one or two decisions the number fed; walk the branch you already pre-named; state what you would measure to fix the assumption for real; keep the wrong number visible and annotated. Better: pre-empt by stating every assumption WITH its sensitivity.

flashcards.q: What should you refuse to estimate?
flashcards.a: p99.9 and anything driven by variance rather than volume: queueing under bursty arrival, GC pauses, lock contention, noisy neighbours, retry amplification. Also anything within 2-3x of a hard cliff (memory limit, provider rate limit, SLO boundary). Instead, design for tail-insensitivity: timeout inside the budget, bulkhead, queue, load-shedding rule.

flashcards.q: The most dangerous number in any estimate.
flashcards.a: The average of a heavy-tailed quantity: average followers, file size, tenant size, request cost, prompt length. Power-law means the mean is smaller than the values that determine capacity, so the estimate understates the peak in exactly the case where the peak breaks you. Ask for a percentile and say the mean will mislead.
